reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: Winsorization pooled across full 56,646-obs panel; Table 1 reports post-winsorize stats.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: Paper Section 3.3, p.536: 'We winsorize all variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles to minimize the influence of outliers. Table 1 provides summary statistics of the key variables used in this study.' The two sentences are adjacent in the same paragraph; the natural reading is that Table 1 reports the winsorized variables. The paper is silent on partition. Independent confirmation that Table 1 is post-winsorize: Cash Flow Panel A shows mean=-0.3758 and SD=4.8386 -- without winsorization, this distribution would have SD an order of magnitude larger (the user's pre-winsorize Formula-A test produced SD~31 on a larger sample); the SD=4.84 is consistent with 1%/99% winsorization having occurred. Caveat: pooled vs by-year/by-industry is not testable from the paper text. The pooled assumption is the package default and the most common literature convention but rests on inference, not paper statement.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED: Winsorize pooled across the full 56,646-observation regression panel. Compute 1st and 99th percentile of each variable on the post-filter sample; clip values to those cutoffs. Table 1 reports post-winsorize statistics. CAVEAT: if pooled winsorization fails to reproduce beta=0.0076 within rounding, run robustness tests with by-fyear and by-industry-year partitions.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: Sample filters applied first, then variables constructed, then winsorization on the post-filter panel.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: Paper narrative order anchors this: Section 3.1 ('Data collection') lists the SIC and AT filters, ending with 'This yields a final sample of 56,646 firm-year observations.' Section 3.3 ('Variables') then introduces variable construction and ends with the winsorization sentence. The phrase 'final sample of 56,646' in Section 3.1 -- before winsorization is introduced in Section 3.3 -- confirms that the 56,646-obs sample is determined by filters, not by winsorization (winsorization does not drop observations, it clips them; the count is unaffected by winsorization regardless of order).
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED: Apply all sample filters first (SIC, AT, missing-value handling, CRSP link, state assignability). Compute all variables on the resulting panel. Then winsorize each continuous variable at the 1st and 99th percentiles of its empirical distribution on this panel.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: R&D=0 and AcqExp=0 when missing (Bates 2009 inheritance); Dividend=0 when missing (paper-explicit); all other controls drop on missing.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: The Bates 2009 inheritance argument is sound -- the paper cites Bates 2009 explicitly (Section 3.3, p.536: 'We follow the literature (Bates et al., 2009; Opler et al., 1999)') and Bates 2009 sets missing XRD and missing AQC to zero by convention. However, the analyst's INDEPENDENT empirical-signature argument has a weakness the analyst overstated: (a) For Acquisition Expenditure: Table 1 Panel A reports p25=0, median=0, p75=0.0144. The >50% zero-mass is consistent with zero-imputation, but it is ALSO consistent with the natural distribution of AQC (most firms don't make acquisitions in a given year, and Compustat AQC=0 is a legitimately reported value for non-acquirers in many years -- not always missing). So the empirical signature is suggestive but not conclusive. (b) For R&D Expenditure: Table 1 Panel A reports p25=0, median=0.0021, p75=0.0738. The median is NOT zero; this means at most 25-50% of the sample has R&D in [0, 0.0021] and clearly less than 50% has exact-zero R&D. The 'zero-mass empirical signature' argument the analyst applied to R&D does NOT hold. R&D zero-imputation is supported ONLY by the Bates 2009 inheritance argument, not by the empirical signature.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: AMENDED OPERATIONAL INSTRUCTION: (a) Dividend Paying Firms(0/1): set to 0 when missing (paper-explicit, no risk). (b) R&D Expenditure: set XRD = 0 when missing (Bates 2009 convention only; the analyst's empirical-signature argument was wrong for R&D, but the Bates inheritance argument and the N=56,646 constraint both support zero-imputation as the only way to reach the published sample size). (c) Acquisition Expenditure: set AQC = 0 when missing (Bates 2009 convention; empirical signature is consistent but not definitive). DIAGNOSTIC: implement R&D=0 first and check N. If N overshoots 56,646, AcqExp zero-imputation may be unnecessary. If N undershoots, both are required.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: AT_{t-1} (BoY) for Cash/CapEx/AcqExp/R&D (explicit in Table A1); AT_t (contemporaneous) for BookLev/MTB/CF/NWC (silent in Table A1).
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: The operational split is correct. Appendix A Table A1 is explicit on 'at the beginning of the year' for Cash, External Debt Financing, External Equity Financing, Capital Expenditure, Acquisition Expenditure, and R&D Expenditure; it is silent on timing for Book Leverage, Market-to-book, Cash Flow, and Net Working Capital. Bates 2009 (NBER WP 12534) verbatim uses contemporaneous AT throughout ('the ratio of capital expenditures (#128) to book assets (#6)' -- no timing qualifier means current-fiscal-year #6). Where Boasiako-Keefe adds 'beginning of the year' they deviate from Bates 2009 deliberately; where they are silent they default to Bates 2009 contemporaneous convention. CHALLENGE TO ANALYST'S RATIONALIZATION: The analyst justified the split as 'flow variables use BoY, stock variables use contemporaneous.' This is post-hoc and breaks for the dependent variable: Cash is a stock (a balance-sheet snapshot) yet is scaled by BoY AT. The clean reading is not stock-vs-flow but 'Bates 2009 default = contemporaneous AT unless the paper explicitly states otherwise.' The operational instruction is unchanged; the underlying justification is just simpler than the analyst implied.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED with rationale correction: Use AT_{t-1} (lagged / beginning-of-year) for: Cash, Capital Expenditure, Acquisition Expenditure, R&D Expenditure, External Debt Financing, External Equity Financing. Use AT_t (contemporaneous / fiscal-year-end) for: Book Leverage, Market-to-book, Cash Flow, Net Working Capital. RATIONALE (corrected): the explicit/silent split in Table A1 is a deliberate signaling choice -- the paper names timing only where it diverges from the Bates 2009 contemporaneous-AT default. There is no clean stock-vs-flow logic; Cash is a stock variable yet uses BoY AT (an Opler-1999-style deviation from Bates 2009).

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: Industry CF Volatility uses backward-looking window [t-10, t-1] excluding year t, >=3 obs floor, FF49 classification.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: Two distinct sub-claims to evaluate: WINDOW TIMING and INDUSTRY CLASSIFICATION. WINDOW TIMING: Table A1 reads 'Standard deviation of industry average cash flows for the previous 10 years; at least 3 years of observations required.' 'Previous 10 years' naturally reads as backward-looking [t-10, t-1] exclusive of t; the analyst's reading is defensible. INDUSTRY CLASSIFICATION: This is where the analyst over-reached. Footnote 5 (p.535) says: 'The industry dummies are constructed based on the 49-industry classification of Fama and French (1997).' This footnote attaches to rho_j in Equation (1), which is the INDUSTRY FIXED EFFECT, not the Industry Cash Flow Volatility control variable. The paper is SILENT on the industry classification used to compute Industry Cash Flow Volatility. Bates 2009 explicitly uses two-digit SIC (NBER WP 12534 verbatim: 'Industry sigma is the mean of standard deviations of cash flow/assets over 10 years for firms in the same industry as defined by two-digit SIC code'). The analyst's claim that Boasiako-Keefe uses FF49 for ICFV is an inference, not paper-stated -- it could equally use 2-digit SIC matching Bates 2009. The Table 1 Panel A summary stat for Industry Cash Flow Volatility (mean=0.3440, SD=0.5270) does not uniquely identify which classification was used.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: AMENDED: WINDOW: backward-looking [t-10, t-1] exclusive of t, >=3 obs floor (endorse). INDUSTRY CLASSIFICATION: PAPER IS SILENT. The analyst's claim that FF49 is used for ICFV is unsupported by paper text; footnote 5's FF49 reference applies only to the industry fixed effect (rho_j), not the ICFV variable. Replication should test BOTH conventions: (a) FF49 for ICFV (analyst's inference, internally consistent with paper's FE scheme); (b) two-digit SIC for ICFV (Bates 2009 verbatim convention). Compare the resulting ICFV summary stats against Table 1 Panel A (mean=0.3440, SD=0.5270) to identify which the paper used.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: Software unidentified, most likely Stata reghdfe; confidence appropriately marked low.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: Adversarial search of the paper turned up no software-identifying clues. Acknowledgments (p.528) thank the managing editor, an anonymous referee, conference participants, and seminar participants but do not mention Stata, R, or any specific package. Footnotes 1-7 contain no software reference. The corresponding author (Michael O'Connor Keefe, michael.keefe@vuw.ac.nz) is at Victoria University of Wellington; his Google Sites page (https://sites.google.com/site/mockeefe/Data) hosts an Online Appendix PDF but no replication code is visible from the landing page. The reported Adj R^2 = 0.4939 for Column (1) is consistent with both reghdfe (which includes absorbed-FE variance in R^2) and areg (which reports only the within-R^2) -- this number is NOT uniquely diagnostic. Authors' prior papers in Stata-heavy fields (corporate finance at VUW) and the multi-way clustered SE in Column (5) (which is straightforward only in modern Stata via reghdfe or in R via fixest) make Stata reghdfe the most likely candidate, but this is inference. ENDORSE the analyst's low-confidence verdict.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED: Most likely Stata reghdfe (or equivalent: R fixest::feols, Python pyhdfe). Cannot be confirmed from the paper text. For implementation, use reghdfe defaults: 'reghdfe Cash DisclosureLaw $controls, absorb(state year industry) cluster(state)'. Equivalent R: 'fixest::feols(Cash ~ DisclosureLaw + controls | state + year + industry, cluster = ~state, data = ...)'. Coefficient and SE will match across packages within numerical precision.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: FE absorption method (dummy variables vs within-transformation) is FWL-equivalent for coefficient identification; affects only reported R^2.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: This is a well-established statistical result (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, 1933/1963). Under OLS, demeaning by category and adding category dummies produce numerically identical point estimates and identical residuals; the only differences are (a) the reported R^2 / Adj R^2 (which depend on whether absorbed-FE variance enters the explained-variance numerator), (b) the degrees-of-freedom adjustment for SE (modern packages handle this correctly), and (c) computational speed. The analyst's claim is correct on the mathematical fact. No adversarial challenge to raise.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED verbatim: Either reghdfe (absorb(year industry state)) or explicit dummy inclusion produces identical point estimates and identical state-clustered SE. Use either. To reproduce Adj R^2 = 0.4939 exactly, use reghdfe defaults (or fixest's default which matches reghdfe). Coefficient on Disclosure Law(0/1) is unaffected by the choice.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: HQ state from Compustat STATE field, applied STATICALLY per gvkey (time-invariant), firms acknowledged as mis-assigned post-relocation.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: The analyst's claim that Compustat STATE is 'static per gvkey, time-invariant' is OPERATIONALLY MISLEADING. In standard WRDS Compustat extracts, there are TWO state fields available: (a) the comp.company header table reports a SINGLE static state per gvkey (most-recent filing); (b) the comp.funda annual fundamentals table reports a TIME-VARYING state per gvkey-fyear (the state recorded in each year's filing). Practitioners must CHOOSE which to use; they are not the same. The paper's text -- Section 3.2, p.535: 'focusing on the states in which firms are headquartered is a conservative approach, since it essentially downward biases beta in Equation (1)' -- is silent on which Compustat state field is used. The 'conservative approach' framing refers to the EXTRA-STATE-EXPOSURE issue (firms operating in multiple states before their HQ state passes), NOT to the FIRM-RELOCATION issue (firms changing HQ state during the sample). These are two distinct biases the analyst conflated.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: AMENDED: HQ state is from Compustat (either company-header or funda-annual). The paper is silent on which. For firms that did NOT relocate during 1997-2015, the choice is immaterial. For firms that DID relocate (~5-10% of the sample), the choice changes treatment-year assignment. Default operational choice: use funda annual STATE (time-varying), which is more faithful to the firm's actual HQ in each year. Document this choice and re-run with static company-header STATE as a robustness check. The paper's 'conservative approach' comment is about pre-exposure to multi-state operations BEFORE home-state law passage, NOT about firm relocations during the sample -- the analyst conflated two distinct issues.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: Treatment dummy = 1 starting fyear >= enactment_year + 1 (not effective_date + 1); matches Beck (2010) and Francis (2014).
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: Paper Section 3.2, p.535: 'Disclosure Law(0/1)_{s,t} is a dummy variable that switches to one the year after the focal state passed the disclosure law.' The phrase 'passed' (not 'effective') refers to enactment / legislative passage. Table A1 corroborates: '1 for periods after the enactment of the state-level data breach notification laws, and 0 otherwise' -- the word 'enactment' is used explicitly. Footnote 3 (p.533) points to NCSL, which publishes both dates; the paper's explicit choice of 'passed' and 'enactment' identifies the date type. The analyst's specific claim about Beck et al. (2010) and Francis et al. (2014) using enactment-year is not directly verifiable from the Boasiako-Keefe paper but is consistent with standard practice in the law-and-finance DiD literature. Section 3.2 itself ties Boasiako-Keefe's setup to these templates: 'Similar to previous studies (Beck et al., 2010; Francis et al., 2014), we use a difference-in-differences approach to examine how firms change their cash policies in response to changes in state-level data breach disclosure laws.'
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED: Disclosure Law(0/1) = 1 when fyear >= enactment_year + 1, else 0. Use the enactment year from the NCSL table referenced in footnote 3 (URL: http://www.ncsl.org/research/telecommunications-and-information-technology/security-breach-notification-laws.aspx). Example: California enacted in 2002, so Disclosure Law(0/1) = 1 for fyear in {2003, ..., 2015} for CA-headquartered firms. Do NOT use effective date. Treatment is determined at the calendar-year level of enactment, not the fiscal-year-end level. CAVEAT: for firms with non-December fiscal-year-end, the enactment-year-vs-fyear mapping may have edge cases; the paper does not address this and any such cases are minor.

reviewer_verdicts.claim_summary: N=56,646 reflects the FULL regression-ready panel (SIC+AT+CRSP-link+state+all-controls-non-missing-with-zero-imputation+ICFV-computable), not just the SIC+AT filters narrated in Section 3.1.
reviewer_verdicts.evidence_for_verdict: STRICT LITERAL READING of Section 3.1 (p.534): the prose lists only 'we collect initial firm-level data from the merged Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP)/Compustat database for the period 1997-2015 ... we exclude all financial firms ... We exclude utility companies ... We further drop observations with negative or missing total book assets. This yields a final sample of 56,646 firm-year observations.' Strictly, 'this yields' refers to these listed filters only -- the analyst's claim that ADDITIONAL implicit filters are folded into 56,646 is not supported by the prose verbatim. HOWEVER, the analyst's reading is ARITHMETICALLY FORCED by an independent constraint: Table 2 Column (1) also reports N=56,646. The regression cannot run without all 11 controls non-missing. Therefore the 56,646 must reflect the all-controls-computable panel, which means the paper's Section 3.1 prose is INCOMPLETE -- it states the explicit filters but the final count baked in additional implicit filters (CRSP-link from 'merged CRSP/Compustat database', state assignability, all controls non-missing with zero-imputation for R&D/AcqExp/Dividend, ICFV computable). The analyst's resolution is correct as an OUTPUT but slightly over-interpreted as paper INTENT: the paper presents 56,646 as if it follows from the listed filters alone, when in fact it must include implicit filters to be consistent with Table 2. This is a common style failing in empirical corporate finance, not a paper error.
reviewer_verdicts.corrected_answer: ENDORSED with annotation: The 56,646 reported in Section 3.1 cannot literally be the product of only the SIC+AT filters listed there -- Table 2 Column (1) reports the same number for the regression sample, which requires all controls non-missing. The analyst's operational reading is correct: N=56,646 is the full regression-ready panel after applying explicit filters (1997-2015, SIC, AT>0) AND implicit filters (CRSP-link, state assignability, all controls computable with R&D/AcqExp/Dividend zero-imputation, ICFV >=3-year minimum, AT_{t-1}>0 for BoY denominators). The paper's Section 3.1 prose omits the implicit filters; readers must back them out from the Table 2 N constraint. Replication diagnostic: if your post-explicit-filter chain yields > or < 56,646 by more than 1-2%, the implicit-filter implementation is wrong and Claim 3's missing-value handling is the most likely culprit.

summary.overall_assessment: The analyst's resolution package is largely safe to code against. No claim is fatally wrong in the sense of producing a coefficient with wrong sign or >2x wrong magnitude. The three amendments are: (3) the empirical-signature argument for R&D zero-imputation does not hold because R&D's median is 0.0021 not zero -- only the Bates 2009 inheritance argument supports R&D=0-if-missing, weakening the evidence (still operationally correct, just thinner support); (5) the analyst inferred FF49 industry classification for Industry Cash Flow Volatility, but the paper's footnote 5 attaches FF49 only to the industry fixed effect (rho_j); the ICFV classification is genuinely unstated and could equally be Bates 2009's two-digit SIC; (8) the analyst's 'static per gvkey' framing for HQ state is operationally misleading because Compustat offers both static (company-header) and time-varying (funda-annual) STATE fields and the paper is silent on which is used. Claim 4 is endorsed on the operational instruction but with a note that the analyst's stock-vs-flow rationalization is post-hoc and breaks for Cash (a stock variable scaled by BoY AT) -- the cleaner reading is 'paper specifies BoY where it deviates from the Bates 2009 contemporaneous-AT default.' The most material amendment is claim 5 (industry classification for ICFV); the others are coding-level clarifications that should not affect the headline beta=0.0076 by more than rounding. The single biggest replication risk is claim 3: if R&D zero-imputation fails to recover N=56,646, the entire sample-construction chain is mis-specified. Run claim 3 first as the diagnostic check; the N-arithmetic constraint from claim 10 will tell you whether you got it right.
